'''William Anthony Perry''' (born December 16, 1962) is a former American professional [[American football|football]] [[defensive tackle]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 10 seasons, primarily with the [[Chicago Bears]]. Nicknamed "'''the Refrigerator'''" due to his size, he played [[college football]] for the [[Clemson Tigers]], winning [[Atlantic Coast Conference football individual awards#Player of the Year|ACC Player of the Year]], and was selected by the Bears in the first round of the [[1985 NFL draft]]. Perry gained popularity during his rookie season as a member of the [[1985 Chicago Bears season|1985 Bears team]] that won the franchise's first [[Super Bowl]] title in [[Super Bowl XX]]. During the season, Perry occasionally played [[fullback (gridiron football)|fullback]] in goal line situations and set the record for the heaviest player to score a touchdown at {{convert|335|lb|kg}}. He remains the heaviest player to score a touchdown in the Super Bowl and has the largest [[Super Bowl ring]] at size 23–25.<ref name="espn.com">{{Cite web |last=Rovell |first=Darren |author-link=Darren Rovell |date=2015-07-29 |title=Big bling: Perry's Super Bowl ring for sale |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/13342007/william-refrigerator-perry-super-bowl-ring-being-sold-auction |access-date=2024-08-13 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>

'''Willie Aaron Anderson''' (born July 11, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[Tackle (gridiron football position)|offensive tackle]] for the [[Cincinnati Bengals]] and [[Baltimore Ravens]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Auburn Tigers football|Auburn Tigers]] and was selected by the Bengals 10th overall of the [[1996 NFL draft]]. A four-time [[Pro Bowl]]er and three-time first-team [[All-Pro]] selection, Anderson played his first 12 seasons with the Bengals.

The 11 [[quarterback pressure]]s Anderson allowed in 2006 were the fourth-fewest pressures allowed by an offensive tackle in a season between 2006 and 2019.<ref>{{cite tweet|user=PFF|author-link=Pro Football Focus|number=1257679453414658049|title=Fewest pressures allowed by OT in a single season since 2006|date=May 5, 2020}}</ref> He was the first [[right tackle]] to be named a first-team All-Pro in three straight seasons since [[Dan Dierdorf]], [[Ron Yary]], and [[Rayfield Wright]] all did it in the 1970s, and the first right tackle to be named to the Pro Bowl in four straight seasons since [[Jackie Slater]]; no right tackle has accomplished those feats since Anderson.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Willie Anderson Named 2023 Pro Football Hall Of Fame Finalist |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/bengals/.amp/allbengals-insiders-plus/willie-anderson-named-2023-pro-football-hall-of-fame-finalist |magazine=[[Sports Illustrated]] |date=2023-01-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230105023101/https://www.si.com/nfl/bengals/.amp/allbengals-insiders-plus/willie-anderson-named-2023-pro-football-hall-of-fame-finalist |archive-date=2023-01-05 |url-status=live |last1=Heltman |first1=Russ}}</ref>

In 2021, Willie Anderson was inducted into the Alabama Sports Hall of Fame.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.ashof.org/honorees/ashof-inductees/ | title=ASHOF Inductees - Alabama Sports Hall of Fame | date=February 14, 2019 }}</ref>

That following year, he became a member of the Ring of Honor induction class of 2022 for the Bengals, joining [[Paul Brown]], [[Anthony Muñoz]], [[Ken Anderson (quarterback)|Ken Anderson]], and [[Ken Riley]].<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.springfieldnewssun.com/sports/curtis-anderson-set-to-be-inducted-into-bengals-ring-of-honor/MEOHBM4HYFEMTBFU32J4F3HUHE/ | title=Curtis, Anderson set to be inducted into Bengals' Ring of Honor }}</ref>

Willie Anderson is the current host of the [https://www.youtube.com/@everythingbigwillieoline "Everything Big Willie Show"] on [[YouTube]] where he tells his NFL Stories along with his guests. Recent guests include Eagles RT [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PSYePNW0-3g&t=531s Lane Johnson], [http://T.%20J.%20Houshmandzadeh T.J. Houshmandzadeh], [[Corey Dillon]], [[Andrew Whitworth]], [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W9KVW0S6XmQ&t=2682s Amarius Mims], and many more.

He trains [[offensive linemen]] from high school to the NFL at the Willie Anderson Lineman Academy.<ref name=ajc/>

'''Willie James Gault''' (born September 5, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 11 seasons with the [[Chicago Bears]] and [[Los Angeles Raiders]]. Considered one of the fastest NFL players of all time,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brodess |first=Doug |date=April 16, 2011 |title=The Top 25 Fastest Players in NFL History |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/665410-the-top-25-fastest-players-in-nfl-history |access-date=March 14, 2024 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}}</ref> Gault was a member of the Bears team that won [[Super Bowl XX]]. He was also a member of the U.S. Olympic team that boycotted the [[1980 Summer Olympics|1980 Olympics]].

Gault played [[college football]] for the [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]] from 1979 to 1982.  He led the Vols in all-purpose yardage as a sophomore, junior and senior,<ref name="records" /> and was named to the [[1982 College Football All-America Team|All-American team]] in 1982.  He still holds numerous school kickoff return records.<ref name=records>[http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/guides/2012/records.pdf Individual Career Records] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304113625/http://www.utsports.com/sports/m-footbl/guides/2012/records.pdf |date=March 4, 2016 }}, UTSports.com. Retrieved: August 8, 2013.</ref>

Gault married his high school sweetheart, writer/author/actress Dainnese Mathis Gault in 1983. They were married from 1983 to 2002 and have two children. His youngest child is rising painter, artist, Gabe Gault <ref>https://canvasrebel.com/meet-gabe-gault/</ref>

Gault is currently pursuing a career as an actor.  He also remains active in [[masters athletics]], setting [[List of world records in masters athletics|world masters records]] in the [[List of world records in masters athletics#100 metres|100 meter]] and [[List of world records in masters athletics#200 metres|200 meter dash]] for the 45–49, the 50–54, and the 55–59 age groups.

'''William Harrison Thomas''' (born August 13, 1968) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] (1991–1999) and [[Oakland Raiders]] (2000–2001) franchises.

Thomas attended [[Palo Duro High School]] and later played [[college football]] at [[Texas A&M University]] for the [[Texas A&M Aggies football|Aggies]]. After college, Philadelphia selected Thomas in the fourth round, 104th overall in the [[1991 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1991 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1991/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He played for the Eagles in nine NFL seasons. His most notable seasons were in 1995 and 1996 which he was selected as a member of the [[National Football Conference|NFC]]'s [[Pro Bowl]] team. After his Eagles contract expired, Thomas signed with the [[Oakland Raiders]] which were coached by former Eagles assistant, [[Jon Gruden]].

Thomas ended his career with 37 [[Quarterback sack|sack]]s and 27 [[interception]]s and is a member of the 20/20 Club. He was also known as an exceptional pass-coverage linebacker during his career.

Thomas was a member of the coaching staff at [[La Salle University]] as a volunteer assistant during the 2007 season.

Thomas formerly resided in the southern New Jersey area with his wife and three sons. As of 2021, he is now divorced and resides in Pennsylvania.{{citation needed|date=July 2024}}

'''Willie James Drewrey''' (born April 28, 1963) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for nine seasons with the [[Houston Oilers]] and [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[West Virginia Mountaineers football|West Virginia Mountaineers]] and was selected in the 11th round of the [[1985 NFL draft]] by the Oilers with the 281st overall pick.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1985 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1985/draft.htm |access-date=2023-10-05 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

Drewrey played [[high school football]] at [[Northern Burlington County Regional High School]].<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20070930004354/http://www.databasefootball.com/players/playerpage.htm?ilkid=DREWRWIL01 Willie Drewrey]}}, database Football. Accessed December 8, 2007.</ref> After graduating high school, Drewrey was an electrifying player for the Mountaineers in the early 80s. He was an ace in the return game and a consistent slot receiver. Drewrey found his niche on special teams at the end of his freshman season. Coach Don Nehlen realized he had to get Willie more touches, giving him increased playing time at wide receiver as his career progressed. Drewrey had a monster senior campaign, ranking 3rd in punt returns, 10th in punt return yardage, and 20th in all-purpose yards. He would be named 1st team All-America that year. In all, Drewrey collected 3,508 career all-purpose yards and 9 touchdowns. He still holds the school record for career punt return yardage 1,191. His special teams capabilities earned him a spot in the NFL for 9 seasons with the Buccaneers (in their creamsicle uniforms) and the Oilers (now the Titans).

'''Willie C. Frazier''' (June 19, 1942 – September 5, 2013) was an American collegiate and professional [[American football]] [[tight end]].   He spent three stints with the [[Houston Oilers]] over a 10-year career in the AFL and NFL and was one of the 4,000-plus plaintiffs in the concussions-related lawsuit against the NFL that was tentatively settled for $765 million a week before his death.

At 6'4", 225 lbs. from [[University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff|Arkansas AM&N]] (now University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff), Frazier played 10 seasons from 1964 to 1975, all in the [[American Football League]] or the [[American Football Conference]] of the [[National Football League]].

Frazier also played tight end for the [[San Diego Chargers]] and the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] between 1964 and 1972 and in 1975.

Born in Eldorado, Ark., Frazier played at [[Arkansas-Pine Bluff]] and joined the AFL's Oilers in 1964. He also played for the Chargers from 1966 through 1970, split the 1971 season between the Chiefs and Oilers and played for Kansas City in 1972 before a final season with Houston in 1975.

He played in 121 games with 209 catches for 3,088 yards, scoring 38 touchdowns, and was selected for the AFL All-Star Game in 1965, 1967 and 1969, winning all-AFL honors with the Oilers in 1965.

Culpepper was noted for his skinny frame at 155 pounds (70 kg) and for his speed.
